items.title: Save on MacBooks, iPads and Apple Watches during October Prime Day
items.summary: Amazon’s October Big Deal Days are underway (lasting through tomorrow night), and we spotted a ton of Apple products and accessories in the sale, ranging from laptops and headphones to desktops and more. Some of the deals are only for Prime members, but other retailers are often
items.content:
Prime Big Deal Days is a great chance to save cash on the latest Apple tech.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Amazon’s October Big Deal Days are underway (lasting through tomorrow night), and we spotted a ton of Apple products and accessories in the sale, ranging from laptops and headphones to desktops and more. Some of the deals are only for Prime members , but other retailers are often matching or beating Amazon’s prices, and we’ll continue to update our coverage as we spot those deals.

If your sights are set beyond what Apple makes, our main roundup has over 100 of the best deals from October Prime Day, and we’re keeping it updated throughout the sale.

The iPhone Air is Apple’s thinnest iPhone yet at 5.6mm, featuring a 6.5-inch ProMotion display, a 48MP fusion camera, and an 18MP front camera with Center Stage support. But its single rear camera and “meh” battery life mean it’s not for everyone.

The iPhone 16E is the spiritual successor to the iPhone SE, bringing flagship-level performance for less than the standard 16. We really wish it included MagSafe for $599, but those upgrading from older iPhones will probably be satisfied with what’s included.

Apple’s second-generation AirPods Max have excellent sound and ANC performance, but are only a minor upgrade from the older pair. Read our review .

The 15-inch Apple MacBook Air features improved performance and better connectivity than the previous generation, and better speakers than the 13-inch model.

The seventh-gen iPad Mini comes with Apple’s A17 Pro chip and support for Apple Intelligence. It’s also compatible with the Apple Pencil Pro and offers faster Wi-Fi and USB-C speeds. Read our review .

A slick 2-in-1 charger that can charge your magnet-friendly iPhone or Pixel at a relatively speedy pace. Its extra charging pad supports AirPods, the Apple Watch, and other Qi-ready accessories.

Slap a recent iPhone onto this charging pad and it’ll charge at fast 25W speeds. It can also charge AirPods, and includes a cord and wall adapter.

The Apple Watch SE 3 is a major glow-up, adding an always-on display, wrist-temperature sensor, a more powerful processor, and fast charging. Read our review.

The AirPods Pro 3 have a new design that improves their fit, superior noise cancellation, better bass, and fairly accurate heart rate sensors. Read our review .

The M4-powered iPad Air excels at AI-powered tasks, and has great battery life, but the 60Hz screen feels underwhelming. Read our review .

Apple’s entry-level iPad is an excellent tablet for casual use, even if it is getting a little long in the tooth. Its high-res screen is great for watching video, and its A16 processor is still fast enough to handle light games and productivity apps. Read our review .

Apple’s recently-updated Mac Mini packs surprising performance into a small package, and the discount helps offset a generational price bump. Read our review .

The newest generation of Apple Watch packs in a variety of upgrades, like faster charging and updated sensors, alongside new Siri and AI features. Read our review .

Apple’s AirPods 4 are last-gen wireless earbuds, but they’re still great. The hard, plastic buds feature improved audio over the third-gen model, along with deep iOS integration and spatial audio with head tracking. Read our review .

This Apple iPhone case features a woven fabric made from recycled polyester for a unique look and rugged protection.

The Apple Pencil Pro arrives with new features like Find My support so you can find the stylus when it gets lost, as well as new creative capabilities like squeeze gestures and the “Barrel Roll” gyroscope.

This keyboard for the iPad turns your tablet into a tiny laptop, and is detachable in case you’d rather just use the kickstand folio cover.

This Speck case features specially designed grips that help prevent accidental drops, and is made from 50 percent recycled plastic.

The Force Case from Casetify comes in a handful of trendy colors, and supports MagSafe accessories and chargers.

items.title: ‘Artificial’ Roasts AI’s Creators—and Sends a Dark Warning About Its Dangers
items.summary: From their dorky parties to their weird walks, the movie holds OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and other stakeholders with contempt, while demonstrating their recklessness.
items.content:
Artificial , the new comedy-drama about OpenAI and the artificial intelligence arms race, is a movie of weird walks.

As OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever, Russian actor Yuri Borisov clomps around, like a geeky Frankensteinian monster. As the controversial OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Andrew Garfield bounces and skips boyishly—a gait that Altman himself recently commended for its accuracy. And as Elon Musk, Ike Barinholtz puts on a loping swagger, commanding rooms of computer nerds like some sort of alpha gorilla (a semblance matched by his long, pouting faces, which call to mind those old Bored Ape NFTs).

During the movie’s post-premiere Q&A earlier this week at the New York Film Festival, Barinholtz wryly described his character as “a person who walks normally.” Such are the awkward saunters of the march of history in the making.

Artificial , directed by Luca Guadagnino, waltzed into NYFF with some controversy clinging to it. The film was originally set to be released by AmazonMGM, which conspicuously dropped it this summer after Amazon struck a $50 billion deal with OpenAI. (Indie house Neon swooped in to pick it up.) NYFF artistic director Dennis Lim referenced “the circumstances” around the film in his onstage introduction.

That OpenAI may have brooked issues with Artificial makes sense. The film is almost completely unflattering, depicting Altman and other OpenAI stakeholders—as well as all the major drivers of the AI boom—as vain, reckless, and insufferably boring. Where 2010’s The Social Network succeeded in making Silicon Valley computer savants look like robust titans of industry and architects of the future, Artificial works to opposing ends. It depicts its tech titans as self-regarding dweebs.

Comparisons to David Fincher’s Facebook drama are inevitable. There’s the subject matter, of course. And the fact that both films feature Garfield in a lead role. (It should be said that Artificial is really more of a biopic of Sutskever, here depicted as both the prime mover of the current AI wave and its nagging moral conscience, than it is of Altman.) But Guadagnino and writer-producer Simon Rich’s approach to the material feels diametrically opposed to Fincher’s. The Social Network was a steely, polished, wordy drama. Artificial is pitched as a black comedy that verges on the surreal.

Guadagnino, best known in Hollywood for the coming-of-age drama Call Me by Your Name and the three-way tennis romance Challengers , has mastered a strain of tense eroticism. There are shades of that in Artificial , in Altman’s seductive wooing of Sutskever’s character. But the film is, for the most part, literally and figuratively sexless.

The images are plain, and even a little ugly. You can almost feel Guadagnino’s more rococo style begging to break out. A slo-mo sequence of a room of gawky programmers dousing each other in bottles of Jarritos, celebrating their AI’s latest self-learning benchmark, is stickily unsexy. A climactic scene of Altman and his OpenAI lackeys confronting Sutskever on a sloping San Francisco street recalls the green-screen backdrops of Tommy Wiseau’s cult classic The Room . After the screening, Guadagnino claimed the story captured a different strain of desire—what he described as “the desire to prevail.”

It’s a need many viewers might share, as leaders in the AI industry (including Altman) appear united in tamping down the technology’s acceleration . Artificial intelligence, we are told, is developing so rapidly, and is becoming so sophisticated, that it risks compromising life on Earth as we know it. In a recent interview with WIRED , former Anthropic AI employee Jacob Coxon alleged that his former colleagues have described the next few years as the potential “endgame” for humanity itself. Another Anthropic researcher claimed that there’s a chance that AI could “kill all humans” within a decade. (The odds were set below 10 percent, which still seems extremely high.)

Artificial stages these tensions as a kind of a high moral drama. Borisov’s well-meaning researcher—depicted as being temperamentally incapable of lying—pleads for safeguards, slow-downs, and AI’s “alignment” with humanity’s broader interests. Meanwhile, the case for exponential technological and capital growth is argued by, well, basically everyone else.

Even the idea of safety itself as saleable. In one scene, concerns about OpenAI’s capacity for serious harm is framed as being beneficial only to the company’s bottom line. Sounding alarm bells signals transparency and due diligence. And the harmful capacity itself is seen as proof positive of the technology’s advancement. It’s win-win. And it’s also no-win.

Artificial makes a persuasive, and frustrating, point about the ongoing AI contest. Pick a metaphor: The train has already left the station, the horses have fled the barn, the toothpaste is out of the tube. The technology already exists. And so, as with nukes in the last century, it becomes not a question of the power itself but who is allowed to harness it, and how. (In his post-Anthropic exit interview, Coxon directly compared the company to the Manhattan Project.)

Questions of ethics become academic, or just annoying, when everyone involved is playing by a different rulebook. If it’s not OpenAI that controls computing’s future, it will be Anthropic, or Google, or Elon Musk. Or, worst of all—at least according to the Trump administration—China. (An early scene in Artificial sees Sutskever and his mentor, Nobel laureate computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton, played by Mark Rylance, rebuff the advances of a Chinese investor eager to use their neural network technology for drones and face-recognition systems.)

items.title: Apple AirPods Max 2 Are $120 Off Right Now During Prime Day (2026)
items.summary: They’re the best over-ear headphones for Apple loyalists, and over 20 percent off at multiple retailers right now.
items.content:
Apple AirPods Max 2 are 22 percent off right now at Amazon, Walmart, and Best Buy. I’ve tested more than 100 wireless earbuds and headphones, and for Apple loyalists, these are the over-ear headphones to get, especially if you bounce between your iPhone and MacBook often. The fact that they’re $120 off the sticker price makes them a much more appealing buy and brings their price closer to options from Sony and Bose.

This isn’t specifically an Amazon Prime Day sale; it’s available at multiple retailers. If you’re curious about other deals happening right now, be sure to check out our guides to the Absolute Best Prime Day Deals , Best Prime Day Apple Deals , and Best Prime Day Headphone Deals .

Apple AirPods Max 2 launched earlier this year, and while they look unchanged from the outside, they have a few key upgrades when you look a little closer.

The biggest is improved active noise-canceling (ANC). AirPods Max were already some of the best ANC headphones you could get—this second version improves on a winning formula with 1.5 times stronger ANC. Having tested this out in the real world, I can confirm they are better at blocking out sound of all kinds.

Other improvements are more software-focused, tied to Apple’s H2 chip inside (upgraded from the H1 in the original AirPods Max). AirPods Max 2 now have many of the features carried over from the latest AirPods Pro, including live translation, adaptive audio, and conversation awareness.

Apple AirPods Pro 3 are also on sale right now at an even better discount than AirPods Max. They also work seamlessly with all your Apple devices, and have a slew of improvements compared to AirPods Pro 2, including better sound quality, noise-canceling, battery life, and water and dust resistance. They also have heart rate sensors built into each earbud so you can track your pulse and calories burned during a workout without a fitness tracker .

items.title: Hark releases an AI personal assistant with a focus on privacy
items.summary: The AI lab's personal assistant is an operating system from the future designed to compete with Muse, Dots, and Instinct.
items.content:
From Muse to Instinct to Dots, tech firms are hunting for the user experience that will make an AI personal assistant a must-have product.

Hark , a startup founded less than a year ago by serial founder Brett Adcock, is throwing its hat in the ring today with the wide release of Hark Pro. Users can access the service for free, with a subscription tier for heavy users.

The company sees its mission as building a user interface for AI, not creating AGI or curing cancer. The foundation is a model trained specifically for computer use, and that’s what Hark Pro does — it uses your computer for you.

That’s perhaps a less ambitious claim than some frontier labs are making, but a little humility goes a long way in winning over users. And rather than an app, Hark’s goal is to create an operating system for the AI computers of our future.

Hark Pro is a full-screen experience with a kind of homepage, featuring a central chat dialog and a feed populated by prompts for actions you might need it to take and visualizations the company calls “panels” that offer mini-dashboards for things you’re interested in. The background is a piece of custom imagery tailored to the weather and time where you are.

Like other AI assistants, users configure it to access their digital life — email, calendar, hard drive, credit cards, etc. Then, it can take on digital tasks as well as fielding classic chatbot questions.

Abidur Chowdhury, a former Apple staffer who leads design at Hark, demoed the product for me. It proactively asked him about expenses he needed to approve, emails he needed to respond to, a meeting with this reporter, and, of course, pointed out that he needed to book a flight for a trip and offered to take care of it. (“I know the flight thing is put to death,” he admits, grinning.)

That does get at the challenge with these apps: One of the harder things for users is actually coming up with useful tasks they are capable of accomplishing. Chowdhury says he was impressed when the AI assistant recently recognized that one of his colleagues needed to renew their car registration at the California DMV, and handled it through the agency’s website.

One notable UX choice that Hark makes is showing the user how the agent navigates the web in a small window, an action most AI assistants perform without it surfacing in the app, which Chowdhury says is intended to build trust with users that the agent is doing the right thing.

That matters because part of Hark’s pitch is that they are not Meta or OpenAI — “we’re not here to like sell you ads and steal your data,” Chowdhury says. To truly leverage these models, users will need to share their entire digital lives. Beyond very real cybersecurity concerns , will users be comfortable with a company like Meta having its products create detailed profiles of their friends and family?

Asked about that kind of profiling, Chowdhury says that “we are doing work to understand you, and be helpful for what you need, but it’s really like task-related — it’s really about how Hark can help take something off your plate and be useful.”

What sets Hark Pro apart from its competitors, Chowdhury says, is its effort to fully subsitute for your computer, but also his belief that it just works better.

“Please compare it to the others, be critical,” he says. “It might not be faster than Muse, but it will give you a better result, and it will work end-to-end instead of asking you to take over at a point.”

One open question is what kind of model best suits the AI personal assistant. Hark’s is explicitly trained for computer use, which makes it faster and cheaper at those tasks, but it’s not clear how much it is trading away the broader knowledge and capability of a frontier LLM.

This software is only half the promise of Hark; Chowdhury made his name designing devices at Apple and Hark promises to release an AI-native device to support its software in 2027.

They’re still cagey about the form it will take, with Chowdhury bemoaning the “creep factor” of wearable cameras. “I will give you this: The first product that we’re building is a product that’s never ever existed before,” he says. We’ll have to wait and see if this is mere hype and Hark puts out some retread tech instead of a truly novel product.

“It’s so hilarious to me that you have AI now, you have a chatbot, and you type stuff in with a keyboard,” Chowdhury says. “Fifty years later and the future of computing is still a terminal.”

items.title: 8 Best Prime Day Wearable Deals: Apple, Google, Samsung (2026)
items.summary: I’ve tested the wearables, tracked the prices, and found the Prime Day deals worth grabbing.
items.content:
This time around, Amazon Prime Day is only two days long, so this is your sign to stop waiting for a better discount. Some of my favorite wearables are on sale, including the latest models and older picks that are hitting their lowest prices yet. Below I’ve rounded up the Prime Day wearable deals I think are worth considering. Every product here has been tested and vetted by WIRED reviewers.

I will be updating this list with the latest Prime Day wearable deals, so be sure to check back regularly. For more information on Prime Day sales, browse our roundups of the Best Prime Day Fitness Deals and Absolute Best Prime Day Deals .

Frankly, I’m surprised to see Apple’s latest watch discounted this soon, so I don’t anticipate this deal sticking around for long. The Apple Watch Series 12 is about $50 off—that may not sound like much, but it’s the lowest price I've seen so far. I bet we’ll see similar discounts around Black Friday, but that’s not a guarantee, so if you want the latest Apple Watch , this sale is a good excuse to add to cart.

Amazon (41 mm and Wi-Fi)

Google (41 mm and Wi-Fi)

Google released its latest Pixel Watch this past summer, and it’s finally on sale. It’s WIRED’s favorite smartwatch for Android users, and it also makes for an excellent fitness and sleep tracker . It’s the second Pixel Watch designed to be repairable, which means you can keep it going for the long haul.

Amazon (GPS + Cellular)

The Apple Watch SE 3 is already the most affordable Apple Watch , and at $199, it’s an even easier sell. It has practically everything the average iPhone user needs from a smartwatch and fitness tracker , granted you’re not an elite athlete or routinely disappearing off the grid. Note that this is the previous-generation model, and Apple didn’t update the SE this year, so you’ll miss out on newer features like Audio Intelligence . Still, with all the features available in the SE 3, it's a tough deal to beat.

After testing the latest Galaxy Watch , I’m here to tell you that Samsung’s previous models still have plenty of life left in them. The Watch8 is down to $220, which is an $80 discount from its original price and, for a limited time, $160 less than its successor. If you want to spend even less, the Watch7 is just $159, which is $91 off its original price and $221 less than the Watch9. You’ll miss out on the newest health metrics, like Antioxidant Index and Heart Health Score, but you’ll still get a durable, well-built smartwatch. Unless you absolutely need the intricate health tracking, save your money and snag one of these deals.

Our budget smartwatch pick is now just $59, which is cheaper than some drop-in fitness classes these days. Don't let the price fool you; the CMF Watch 3 Pro is feature-packed, with wrist-based controls, a built-in mic for voice calls, and a voice assistant. It's also designed with a comprehensive suite of health and fitness metrics, plus dual-band GPS for more accurate route tracking. Plus, it’s got plenty of personality with its retro-futuristic aesthetic.

This Casio doesn’t go on sale often, and while a $24 discount may not seem like much, the lowest price I’ve seen it drop to is $185, so it’s a relatively solid deal. It’s editor Julian Chokkattu ’s favorite solar-powered smartwatch with a bright LCD screen and durable build.

Yes, there’s a newer RingConn Gen 3, but you don’t necessarily need it. The Gen 2 Air is down to $159, which saves you $40 off its retail price and $190 compared with the latest model. You don’t get the advanced metrics like vascular trends and sleep apnea pattern insights, but you’ll still get a capable entry-level smart ring with up to 10 days of battery life.

items.title: Our first five impressions of Googlebooks — exciting but underbaked
items.summary: Googlebooks are here. The first models went on sale Sunday, October 4th, and we received review units of all five Googlebooks about 24 hours ago. Since then, we've been in a mad dash to put the devices through their paces and get a check on what it's like to use these Android lap
items.content:
Google’s new laptop OS shows lots of promise for Android phone owners, but there’s a long road ahead.﻿

Googlebooks are here . The first models went on sale Sunday, October 4th, and we received review units of all five Googlebooks about 24 hours ago. Since then, we’ve been in a mad dash to put the devices through their paces and get a check on what it’s like to use these Android laptops.

At first glance, Googlebooks feel very Chromebook-ish, and at times a little janky. But Google has some great new ideas afoot on how a laptop and phone interact. You can already link your phone to a Windows laptop to sync your notifications and mirror your whole iPhone on macOS. But Googlebooks allow you to take actions on your phone from your laptop in a way that feels natural. When it works, of course.

Here are all the things we’re learning, feeling, and thinking about so far with Googlebooks. The good, the bad, and the weird.

Googlebooks revolve around using an Android phone, and Google’s execution here is great. Setting up a Googlebook with an Android phone is simple and painless. The out-of-box experience is pretty intuitive, prompting you to pair your phone by scanning a QR code, sign into your Google account, and then download some of the apps you’ve already installed on your phone. It’s similar to the most recent Chromebooks, but it’s intuitive.

Casting apps from your phone, migrating a task from your phone to your laptop with a single click, accessing your phone files on your laptop, and getting your phone notifications on your laptop all work well. These are smart ideas that let you keep your focus on your laptop while you work, but some of them are rough around the edges — in some cases, literally.

App casting allows you to use your phone apps directly on a Googlebook, and it feels natural to launch them straight from an app drawer on a laptop instead of mirroring your whole phone screen. But it also means your two separate app drawers on a Googlebook will have duplicate apps. And there’s nothing to stop you from running a desktop version and mobile version at the same time — even with Chrome. That should be easily ignorable, but clicking on synced notifications (like Slack) can open a casted app instead of a web app or native app on the Googlebook. And casted apps sometimes have pixelated text or oddly proportioned UI. They also look and feel just a touch sluggish in animations and scrolling compared to the native desktop apps.

Google’s Continue On feature, which temporarily pins an app you’re using on your phone to the Googlebook taskbar, is super neat. If I open a spreadsheet on my phone, I can easily transfer it over to the laptop with one click. Brilliant! Except, most apps I tried don’t sync over to the Googlebook with that functionality — not even Google Maps or Calendar. It seems mostly for Google Docs and Sheets for now, and it’s awesome for those.

Lastly, pulling files directly off your phone from your laptop just works. It’s great!

I love a fancy light show. Google’s Glowbars on these laptops offer Googlebooks a signature flair, but they don’t do much. It’s on the lid, facing away from you, and it’s normally illuminated white while you use the laptop. It alternates colors when you talk to Gemini, and closing the lid temporarily displays a Google-y rainbow before it sleeps.

The most useful function is that it shows the laptop charge level. But I was hoping for some cool animated lights to show a trickling charge while you have the lid closed or something. It just pulses a few times with green, yellow, or red light to give an approximate charge level when you plug in or unplug a power cable. And the Glowbar that actually faces you on Lenovo’s optional AI Mouse is just a glorified RGB strip that you pick the colors for — it doesn’t sync up to the lid lights.

These little light strips are just begging to be tinkered with. I hope Google does much more here. At least start by showing a constant charge level that slowly fills up the strip.

I love that Google is now flagging Play Store apps with desktop ratings. Browsing apps on a Googlebook classifies them in five categories: Made for desktop, Optimized for desktop, Compatible with desktop, Better on the website, and Built for mobile. We haven’t found many “Made for desktop” apps outside of core Google ones and a few other examples like CapCut Pad and BandLab.

“Optimized for desktop” and “Compatible with desktop” designations seem a little loose. Apple Music is optimized, but it doesn’t respond to right-clicks — only a click-and-hold brings up a context menu. And Firefox is compatible, which means it “works with standard mouse and keyboard controls,” yet it doesn’t respond to keyboard shortcuts for creating, deleting, or switching tabs. As expected, Googlebooks are best used with Google’s Chrome.

An app like Slack, which is acknowledged as “Better on the website,” is best used as a progressive web app install — just as it was on ChromeOS. But the web app couldn’t be installed at first while following the usual procedure I know from Chromebooks. After several attempts and starting from scratch by loading up slack.com , Chrome eventually prompted me to install it.

If I never heard of Googlebooks and you dropped me in front of one of these laptops I’d figure ChromeOS just got a nice upgrade. They feel very Chromebook-ish. That’s not really a bad thing, as I’ve enjoyed Chromebooks for their relatively fuss-free web use. But that also means Googlebooks come with some old trappings of ChromeOS.

Just like on Chromebooks, Chrome on Googlebooks doesn’t support separate Google accounts. You can have multiple Google accounts signed into the Googlebook, but there’s no wall between their browsing, bookmarks, and settings on Chrome like on Windows and macOS.

items.title: OpenAI Is Pissing Off a Bunch of Mathematicians—Again
items.summary: “There’s a perception of mobster behavior” from leading AI companies, one mathematician tells WIRED as OpenAI prepares to release more than 100 new solutions to unsolved problems.
items.content:
In August, OpenAI convened around 40 mathematicians to discuss what to do if AI outpaces human capabilities in the field. The company hinted that its powerful models had solved hundreds of long-standing math problems, say people who were in attendance, but company representatives assured attendees it would not release the solutions all at once—an assurance OpenAI spokesperson Lindsay McCallum says the company is “not aware of”—and, worried by how the community might react, sought advice on how to publish the findings.

Attendees responded with “a mixture of excitement and dread,” but the meeting was a promising first step, recalls Northwestern University mathematician Bryna Kra. The group, she tells WIRED, asked the firm not to just publish them in a blog or tweet, like they had done with 10 problems earlier that month . Instead, it would be important for OpenAI to publish papers explaining the work so that mathematicians could absorb, digest, and use the results, according to Kra. “Apparently, that input was ignored,” she says.

OpenAI has told people it plans to dump hundreds of results to unsolved problems on GitHub on Tuesday, people familiar with the plans tell WIRED. The release would be the latest of tens of thousands of mathematical solutions generated by AI this year, as frontier models become increasingly capable.

“On August 28, we began training a new internal model. In addition to resolving the Navier—Stokes Millennium Prize problem⁠, this model has now resolved more than 100 long-standing open problems across most areas of mathematics,” says McCallum. “We are working to responsibly release the next math results from our model, drawing on advice and public recommendations from the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence at the Institute for Advanced Study to inform how we release these results. We have not set a release time.”

But for several leading mathematicians, the impending output is also a sign that the company has learned little from the controversies over previous releases.

In conversations with WIRED, the academics say they feel the field has become a playground for OpenAI and its rival Anthropic to show off their models as both prepare for blockbuster initial public offerings. In their rush to outdo each other, mathematicians say, traditional scientific processes for releasing and attributing results have been cast aside.

The most striking case so far came in September. OpenAI deployed thousands of agents to solve a legendary million-dollar Millennium Prize problem after hearing “rumors” that others were closing in on solutions. Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician and professor at New York University, accused the company of front-running the work he had done toward solving an element of the problem in a personal collaboration with Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge. The pair hadn’t published their work but had been using OpenAI’s tools to help them.

During an attempt to negotiate credit, Buckmaster claims, OpenAI researcher Sébastien Bubeck seemed to imply that Alpöge should be excluded from any paper, since that would make things complicated. (In response to a request for comment, Bubeck pointed to a previous public statement in which he denied asking for Alpöge to not be listed as an author.) Buckmaster said he refused. In a call, Bubeck claimed that there is some worry about what Anthropic is doing, according to meeting notes seen by WIRED. Levent must be talking to his leadership right now letting them know fucking OpenAI can get a Millennium Prize problem, he said, per the notes. What’s to stop Anthropic from giving all their compute to get a Millennium Prize problem?

According to the notes, Bubeck also seemed to suggest that Buckmaster would be ruining his career when Buckmaster threatened to tell the press about his belief that OpenAI had stolen his work. If you don't want me to be nice, then I don't have to be nice , Bubeck said, according to the meeting notes.

Nestor Guillen, a visiting math professor at NYU, tells WIRED that “there's a perception of mobster behavior” from the AI companies among mathematicians.

“We disagree with that characterization,” says McCallum.

“I feel a lot of angst, and I see this more and more in my colleagues in mathematics, not over AI, but over the AI companies,” Guillen says. “I think a lot of the angst is about the accumulation of power in one place.”

OpenAI assembled an advisory group in mid September to help determine how the company assesses and communicates new results, upholds academic and professional standards, and builds tools that support mathematical research and learning. But the company doesn’t seem to have made much progress, mathematicians say.

Many are frustrated that OpenAI and Anthropic continue to release results through blog posts, rather than scientific papers, which makes them harder to verify and often excludes prior work from other mathematicians. Piecemeal announcements aren’t limited to the labs: Alpöge himself announced he had disproved an 87-year-old conjecture through a tweet sent shortly after the World Cup final.

“Math by tweet and math by press release to me is not the way to nurture the ecosystem that created the fertile ground that they have trained on,” says Kra.

Some have set up new tools this year in reaction to the increase in machine-assisted proofs; the idea is to help the community both use new results and sort through what needs to be further digested. The tools include Hexagon, a repository for primarily AI-generated material, and Palomar, a registry of machine-verified mathematics.

While OpenAI has been directly encouraged to use these tools, “they haven't changed their behavior,” Kra notes. Nor does she feel the company’s actions are aligned with the Leiden declaration , a call by more than 4,000 mathematicians for AI companies to meet mathematicians’ standards that she helped write.

items.title: Apple TV’s great year continues with Small Prophets
items.summary: Apple TV has had a really great run in 2026 - and a cozy new addition is helping expand its lineup even more. As the streaming service has attempted to grow in order to better compete with the likes of Disney and Netflix, it has steadily broadened the range of its series. This ye
items.content:
A quirky supernatural comedy is the latest welcome addition to the streaming service.

Apple TV has had a really great run in 2026 — and a cozy new addition is helping expand its lineup even more. As the streaming service has attempted to grow in order to better compete with the likes of Disney and Netflix , it has steadily broadened the range of its series. This year has included everything from a pair of OnlyFans dramedies to the horror-comedy hybrid Widow’s Bay , alongside the return of some big names like Ted Lasso and Silo . And now you can add Small Prophets to the growing list of new flavors on Apple TV.

The six-episode comedy actually premiered on the BBC earlier this year, but it’s going to be streaming on Apple TV on October 7th. It’s a smart, silly, sweet, and occasionally stressful show, and also one tinged with just a bit of the supernatural. Sort of like British humor meets magical realism. The show centers on Michael Sleep (Pearce Quigley), who has been living like something of a hermit since his girlfriend Clea disappeared without a trace seven years ago. He’s essentially put his life on hold waiting for her to return: He works a job he hates at a hardware store, helps take care of his elderly father (Michael Palin), and lives in a house still stuffed with old boxes full of Clea’s things.

Then one day his dad has an idea: He tells Michael a secret, alchemical recipe that will let him grow tiny magical beings that can answer any question. And since Michael is desperate to know the answer to one particular question — will he ever see Clea again? — he decides to try it, despite not really believing it will work.

What follows is chaotically comical. Michael ends up partnering with his curious coworker Kacey (Lauren Patel) to grow the creatures, called homunculi, but at the same time his previously simple life becomes much more complex. Michael’s father keeps getting into trouble at his nursing home, his neighbors keep threatening to call the council because of his messy yard, and Clea’s broke brother Roy (Paul Kaye) is trying to claim the house so he can sell it and get out of debt. All the while, the homunculi are growing in both size and power.

The best word to describe Small Prophets is charming. Much of this comes down to Michael himself. While he seems like an isolated shut-in on the surface, with his big beard and aloof personality, he’s actually incredibly funny and even lovable… at least to the people he likes. He’s constantly cracking jokes and helping out his small group of family and friends. To everyone else he’s a bit of an asshole, but in a weirdly funny way, like how he constantly shushes his boss so he can take personal calls at work. At one point he impersonates Santa Claus to get out of a mugging. And there’s a bittersweet note to his always-on humor, as Michael does all of this while holding onto the unlikely possibility that Clea is still out there.

It’s a low-key show, but one that is also extremely strong in basically every regard, with an excellent supporting cast, just the right amount of mystery, and the perfect mix of sweet and silly tones. The goofy and heartwarming nature of Small Prophets also makes it a particularly good fit for Apple TV, since there’s nothing else quite like it on the service. It slots nicely between Ted Lasso , which is comforting in a much more overbearing way , and Widow’s Bay , which similarly mixes comedy with the supernatural, but with an end goal of horror . Small Prophets , on the other hand, is much more whimsical; even the homunculi themselves look more like stop-motion puppets than anything scary.

For a long time the major complaint about Apple TV was that it simply didn’t have enough shows. Once you were done with the big names, like Severance or Slow Horses , there wasn’t a whole lot else to watch. But slowly and steadily that has changed, and 2026 has marked something of a turning point for the streaming service. Part of this comes down to a large number of returning shows, from Sugar to Dark Matter , that have further built out the library. But a lot of it has to do with new shows like Small Prophets that are able to fill in those gaps while also broadening the scope of what’s available on Apple TV.

The good news is that this trend looks to continue, at least for the foreseeable future. The next few months of Apple TV include a serial killer thriller ( Nocturne ), a heist drama ( 12 12 12 ), and one of the service’s most ambitious sci-fi shows to date ( Neuromancer ). And as for Small Prophets ? It ends with a promising “to be continued.”

items.title: Mirror Particle is building a ‘world model’ of human behavior
items.summary: Mirror Particle will launch at TechCrunch Disrupt's Startup Battlefield 200 with a world model built from scratch to predict human behavior, arguing that LLM role-play falls short for market research and brand strategy.
items.content:
Startups that promise to predict how humans will behave are having a moment. Over the past year, Simile raised $200 million at a $2 billion valuation; Aaru raised $88 million at a $1 billion valuation; and Humans&, an AI startup that announced a massive $480 million seed round in January at a $4.48 billion valuation, launched Persimmon to model human behavior.

The status quo for human behavior prediction today relies heavily on large language models (LLMs) that are prompted or fine-tuned to role-play as a target demographic. But two-year-old, San Francisco-based Mirror Particle thinks that approach is fundamentally broken.

“It’s like bringing a super soaker to Niagara Falls,” says Abhivyakti Ahuja, co-founder and CEO of Mirror Particle, which provides brands with an AI engine that predicts consumer behavior and the reasons behind it. “LLMs have been trained on hundreds of billions of data points. How much can you influence its behavior by [fine-tuning] with such a small amount of data? It’s still stuck in the past.”

Ahuja doesn’t think LLMs see the world the way a human does. “LLMs are modeling written language, but humans are made of visual perception, spatial reasoning, social intelligence.” Relying on them, she says, means getting insights based on what humans don’t notice, which is beside the point when trying to predict human behavior.

Mirror Particle is taking another approach: building a foundation model, or as Ahuja describes it, a world model built from scratch that simulates why humans do what they do and how human behavior changes over time.

“We don’t want to capture the static person,” Ahuja said. “We want to capture the changing person. That means capturing the longitudinal data on how people are changing, what triggers are changing them and to what degree.” If they aren’t changing, she added, “that’s also a signal.”

Mirror Particle has already raised an angel round and says it’s close to closing its first venture round. The company is also competing next week in Startup Battlefield 200 , TechCrunch’s renowned startup competition taking place at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 in San Francisco on October 13-15.

The startup relies on a proprietary combination of data that includes its clients’ customer data, current events, pop culture, social media, and more to model a demographic segment, thinking of it as a system that evolves over time and tracking how motivations shift as it moves through experiences. Much of the focus is on “revealed behavior” — what people actually do rather than self-reported survey answers.

Like its rivals, Mirror Particle’s initial go-to-market strategy focuses on where budgets already exist for these kinds of insights: market research and brand and product strategy. Mirror might, for instance, help a beauty brand not just write better ad copy for makeup that would appeal to Gen Z, but also determine if that demographic even wants that product.

“What if [the target demographic] doesn’t want eyeshadow palettes?” Ahuja said. “Maybe blush is a better option to go for if you want to sell a product to this market.”

Mirror Particle’s prediction engine also provides customers with the “why” behind current or future behavior — the motivations, constraints, and additional context that justify its recommendation, helping brands make smarter decisions.

In one early pilot, a well-known pet food brand wanted to know what imagery to put on the packaging to boost sales. Chicken? Beef? Vegetables? Mirror’s technology found that the brand was asking the wrong question. The imagery didn’t matter. The problem was that the brand was so recognizable that it was considered mass market and cheap, and sales would plateau until it addressed that perception issue.

“The way we see our model evolving is like how a baby learns about the world,” Ahuja said, noting that babies move from vision to language to body awareness to social intelligence.

That fundamental interest in modeling the human brain comes from Ahuja’s background studying neuroscience and computer science. Originally from India, she ended up studying at the University of Toronto, where she became inspired by AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton’s contributions to neural networks.

After school, Ahuja ended up at Amazon Robotics building robots that build other robots. That’s where she met her co-founders, Will Song and Thomson Yen. Song has spent a chunk of his career building sales personalization engines, and Yen focused on using deep learning to learn about how AI agents understand human behavior.

The startup’s long-term vision is to be the “general layer for anticipating human behavior” and moving from broader population-level analyses to individual-level insights.

“We just need a better model of humans if we’re going to work alongside AI and with each other,” Ahuja said.

Check out Mirror Particle and many other innovative startups that have been vetted by TechCrunch’s editorial team next week at Disrupt in downtown San Francisco . The winner of this year’s Startup Battlefield will be decided by our slate of VC judges on the afternoon of Thursday, October 15.

items.title: Learn all about scaling, fundraising, founder how-tos, and more at TechCrunch Founder Summit, November 4
items.summary: There isn’t a single manual to read or prompt to give an LLM that can equip you with the skills and knowledge to build a company. But on November 4, TechCrunch Founder Summit gives founders the next-best thing: A packed day at Boston's SoWa Power Station, where investors and oper
items.content:
There isn’t a single manual to read or prompt to give an LLM that can equip you with the skills and knowledge to build a company. But on November 4, TechCrunch Founder Summit gives founders the next-best thing: A packed day at Boston’s SoWa Power Station, where investors and operators share how they’ve navigated crucial decisions. The Founder Summit’s agenda is built around core questions every founder eventually has to answer about capital, leadership, and what they’re actually building toward. And each session is designed to build upon each other. Like your startup’s founding team, these sessions work together to drive outcomes.

This is a breakdown on how the full event agenda fits together, and what you can expect to learn by attending. Keep in mind that tickets are at their lowest price point before they increase on October 16, so this is the ideal moment to grab your seat. You can save $200 on both Investor and Founder passes up until that deadline.

For a limited time, you can also get a second ticket for 50% off, and for even larger groups, there are bundle discounts available to groups of four or more.

Fundraising advice often stops at “How do I get the term sheet?” This track goes further, because getting a yes is only half of the equation. The other half is making sure it’s the right yes.

Underscore partner Brian Devaney opens with a candid read on today’s fundraising climate, including what investors are actually screening for right now, how founders can differentiate in a crowded market, and the specific moments where founders give up leverage without realizing it.

That’s the part most founders obsess over — as well as who ends up on the cap table once the round closes. This is where Vineet Edupuganti , co-founder and CEO of Cogent Security , picks up the thread. After raising an $11 million round, he learned firsthand that not every check is equal. He’ll walk through how to actually evaluate investors and navigate those trade-offs before you sign, not after.

This all frames fundraising as a two-part decision. First, win the leverage in the room, then spend it wisely on the right partners. Founders who only solve the first part often find themselves fighting their own cap table later.

Grab your pass and get all these fundraising insights. Bring your co-founder at 50% off.

No founder stays the same kind of leader forever. After all, the skills that get a company to its initial customers rarely match what’s needed when its customer list expands and the employee count grows. This track tackles that shift from two angles: the founder’s evolution, and the decisions on employees that either support or sabotage it.

HubSpot co-founder and Sequoia partner Brian Halligan has experienced this arc many times, first by building through HubSpot’s own stages of growth and now by advising founders doing the same from the investor’s seat. He’ll unpack how the CEO job transforms at each stage, the leadership habits that stop working once a company outgrows them, and how to keep reinventing yourself without losing what made you effective in the first place.

But a founder’s evolution doesn’t happen in isolation — it’s constrained by who’s actually in the building. NEA partner Melissa Taunton brings the hiring half of that equation, breaking down how early team decisions quietly set the ceiling on a company’s culture, speed, and ability to execute long before anyone notices the cracks. The founders who scale smoothly, in her experience, are the ones who treat early hires as architecture decisions, not just headcount.

Get your ticket, learn the skills every founder needs, and bring a teammate along.

This is the track where the agenda gets most forward-looking, and it’s really three questions in sequence: What are you building, do people actually want it, and will it be big enough to matter?

7AI co-founder and CEO Lior Div starts with the “what.” Adding AI features to an existing product is a tactical decision, and building a company where AI is the foundation from day one is a structural one, touching everything from team composition to how go-to-market actually works. He’ll explore what founders need to rethink when AI isn’t a feature, but the premise.

Next, Kent Bennett from Bessemer Venture Partners tackles the question, “Do people want it?” This is a necessary gut check right after a session on ambitious AI-native building: It’s easy to mistake early traction or investor enthusiasm for real product-market fit. He’ll unpack the signals that genuinely indicate fit and the metrics that mislead founders into scaling too early.

Finally, TDK Ventures investment director Tina Tosukhowong zooms out to the category level with an explanation of the firm’s “King of the Hill” framework, which is the discipline top investors use to judge whether a company isn’t just viable, but also positioned to define its entire category on economics, scalability, and timing. It’s the lens that explains why some well-built, well-funded products never break out, while others soar to success.

Get ahead of the race to make the most of AI tools to build and register today.

It’s one thing to hear these ideas in the abstract. HqO co-founder and CEO Chase Garbarino closes the agenda as a working example of all three tracks at once. After all, he’s raised $200 million from the right investors, scaled a team across more than 30 countries, and built a category-defining company, all without ever relocating from Boston.

He’ll break down the real advantages and disadvantages of building outside a major hub, and what every founder outside Silicon Valley should know before assuming they need to be somewhere else.

items.title: Googlebook "Better Together" phone features don't work with Samsung at launch
items.summary: Googlebooks require Android 17, but Samsung's Android 17 phones won't work yet.
items.content:
Googlebooks are Google’s latest attempt to carve out a piece of the premium laptop market, and tight integration with Android phones is a key part of that effort. Now that Googlebooks are available, we’re learning of some frustrating limitations of that plan. For now, Googlebooks will only play nicely with your phone if you have a Pixel.

When Google announced the launch window for Googlebooks, it said the laptops were “engineered to work with your Android phone right out of the box.” But as with many things Google, the truth is more convoluted. We have since learned that you need Android 17 for any of the nifty integrations to work. With a compatible Android 17 phone, you can seamlessly stream apps to your laptop, access files on your phone, mirror notifications, and continue where you left off in certain apps when switching from phone to laptop.

You might think that the latest Samsung phones, which shipped with Android 17, would be ready for this experience. You’d be wrong, though. Some early Googlebook adopters have complained that phones like the Z Fold 8 won’t work with the laptops. While the devices appear to see each other, the phone doesn’t stay connected. Google representatives have since confirmed that these “Better Together” features are not currently supported on even the latest Samsung phones. An update that brings support to Samsung phones will roll out in “the coming weeks.”

Even when that update arrives, only Samsung phones with Android 17 will work. If you have an older or cheaper phone, you may not get the necessary OS update until later. And Samsung is actually better about update support than most device makers. Motorola released its 2026 phones with Android 16, and they’re still waiting on a final update to version 17. OnePlus, which has recently scaled back its operations in several markets, is also still testing Android 17. Xiaomi has rolled out Android 17 to some high-end devices, but Googlebooks aren’t available in most of its core markets.

This leaves Pixel phones as the only option if you want proper mobile integration with your new Google laptop today. The Googlebook platform probably appeals more to people who already use the company’s bespoke Android phones, but Samsung is by far the largest Android OEM. Launching Googlebooks without Samsung support, and not being clear about that in any public statements, is not a great start for Google’s refreshed laptop effort.

The core issue is that Googlebooks rely on features that are exclusive to Android 17. This used to be a common issue with Android, as phones from various manufacturers often lag behind on major OS updates. However, Google has worked to move more features into Google Play Services and create a modular system layer to accelerate updates. The result is that you don’t usually have to care what build of Android your phone runs anymore—there are very few features exclusive to new versions today, but Googlebook support is apparently one of them.

items.title: Anthropic is giving startups a free year of Claude Team and $1,000 in credits
items.summary: "We created this program because we believe the benefits of AI will reach most people through the companies that build on top of models, rather than through the models alone."
items.content:
On Tuesday, Anthropic announced an expansion of its Claude for Startups program, offering subsidized access to its AI models and a variety of other benefits to qualifying companies.

The new version of the program, which launched as part of Anthropic’s SF Tech Week event , provides a free year of Claude Team, Anthropic’s paid plan for groups, with up to five premium seats, as well as $1,000 in API credits for building with Claude. Companies will also get access to Claude Marketplace, which lets them build plug-ins for the service. Companies can also book virtual office hours with Anthropic’s Applied AI team.

“We created this program because we believe the benefits of AI will reach most people through the companies that build on top of models, rather than through the models alone,” Anthropic said in an announcement. “That makes partnering closely with founders and developers central to our mission.”

Companies are eligible if they were founded in the last five years or received funding in the last two years. Interested companies can apply through the Claude for Startups program page.

items.title: LibreOffice says ‘no AI’ is now a software feature
items.summary: The maker of the open source document editor says it has no plans to add AI to its software's default configuration, citing user privacy.
items.content:
If you’re looking for a document editor that doesn’t use artificial intelligence, LibreOffice may be just the software for you.

The Document Foundation, the nonprofit software maker behind the open source document editor LibreOffice, said in a blog post this week that while it does not reject AI out of hand, it “will not add” AI to its software for the foreseeable future.

The blog post comes weeks after the release of the latest version of LibreOffice in late August, in which the nonprofit reiterated that the software “contains no generative AI features.”

LibreOffice said at the time that this was a “deliberate design position” to ensure that users’ documents are not uploaded to a server for processing and that no part of the software requires a network connection to function. The nonprofit added that its software is used by tens of millions of people and organizations, and that users should retain control over their data.

“Any organisation handling confidential, legally privileged or personal data needs to know where that data goes, and the only assurance that survives an audit is that it does not leave the machine,” the organization said.

LibreOffice says users can still choose to use AI tools by installing software extensions that connect the document editor to local AI models.

The decision to eschew including AI features bucks the trend of many software makers today that try to pack in as much AI as possible, even to the detriment of the user experience. The so-called “enshittification” of modern software by packing in unnecessary and bloated features, like chatbots and AI assistants, prompted some developers to create or include features that block or remove AI features altogether.

AI tools often require the users’ data to be uploaded and processed on a remote server, which the user has no control over how the data is stored or for how long.

LibreOffice said that there is currently “no integration” that meets all of its requirements, such as ensuring that the users’ data stays on their device and that there is no reliance on a single AI provider, among other considerations. The organization’s criteria for including AI into its software is not a “definitive rejection,” but the decision was an assessment of the technology today, rather than a “judgement on the value of the sector.”

“Until then, there will be no AI of any kind in the default installation; extensions will be available for those who wish to integrate AI features, and we will closely monitor where the technology is actually heading,” said LibreOffice’s blog post .

LibreOffice is one of the many kinds of open source and alternative software used to escape the clutches of Silicon Valley tech giants.

items.title: Vinod Khosla believes ex-DeepMind engineer’s Wajo will win agent market on trust
items.summary: Wajo's Fo agent can hire humans to complete a task.
items.content:
The personal-agent space has become closely competitive in recent weeks, with Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dot, and Instinct taking the lead and more competitors being launched each week . But Vinod Khosla is betting on former Google and DeepMind engineer Shivani Poddar’s Wajo for one simple reason: trust.

“I think the most important thing in an agent, because it’s acting for you, is trust. You have to have trust in the agent, and I think compared to either Muse or Instinct, Wajo is the most trustworthy because it is architected to focus on trust and safety first, and some of the others are not,” Khosla told TechCrunch over a call.

“I mean, who wants to give all their data to Facebook [Meta]? I don’t. And if I give my data to Facebook, I’m the product, not the product I am buying, because they are in the ad business. So trust is important, and most people don’t trust a large company like Facebook,” he added.

In broad strokes, Wajo’s Fo agent works very much like Muse or Instinct. The agent can work across iMessage and WhatsApp, and has a web interface with cards of potential tasks. Errands are organized into categories like “scheduling,” “gifting,” and “life admin.” Its agent can also call businesses or other people on your behalf, booking or canceling services as needed.

In a few early tests, I asked it to call an airline to check for upgrades, and it successfully did so. However, when I asked it to call my partner and remind her to feed the cats, the call didn’t go smoothly, and disclosures were less clear. As rivals like Instinct and Muse are also rolling out calling ability slowly, we might see more discussions around how an AI calling on someone’s behalf should disclose itself. One of the unique things about the tool is that it can hire a human to complete a task when needed.

Apart from this, Fo can create a virtual credit card and pay on your behalf without disclosing your details. The agent also has its own email and can converse with people and businesses. When websites or services block AI agents, Fo can inform the user to take action or create a group with the user and the business for verification.

The startup has also secured backing from Jeff Dean and Gokul Rajaram, but didn’t specify the money raised. Wajo didn’t provide any numbers around users but said that it’s being used in 107 countries and has grown 10x since its launch in late September.

Prior to founding Wajo, Poddar worked in various engineering roles at Meta, Google, and DeepMind and was invovled in making the first Facebook assistant. She said that she wanted to build products that were useful to people.

“The whole journey of bringing Gemini to the world and building safety for it made me realize the technological depth that you need to do this. Google is so good in technology that sometimes it can be left behind in product. I thought I needed to do something that is both technology and product at the same time. It has to be something different, which is very grounded in what the user needs,” Poddar told TechCrunch over a call.

The former Google engineering lead mirrored Khosla’s thoughts around trust, and emphasized that it was one of the core principles for Wajo.

“Trust is something you have to build from the get-go because one of the technological things that has not been solved yet is teaching agents to unlearn. If they get access to your personal data on day zero, they will always have it for the future. I think trust needs to be built from day zero, not only in your architecture, but in product choices,” she said.

The company is doing work in a few areas in relation to trust and safety. It has applied for a patent for its virtual card system that hides users’ information from sites. For calls, the company said it will include a “trusted contact” list for users whose agents can call them. When you get a call, you can also tell the agent not to call you again, and Wajo records that preference.

In the meantime, wajo’s Fo has a tos complaint solution to agents on Amazon folks. Shop on :) https://t.co/yx2SoknZIy

The startup’s challenge is not to raise privacy concerns like other agents, especially as it is marketing safety as a core value. It also claims that despite tools like Muse being blocked by Amazon , its architecture follows the e-commerce service’s terms of service.

Wajo said that in the coming months it will explore how its Fo agent will work in social settings across multiple users, with the core idea of keeping privacy intact.
